subtopic: Significant Figures and Errors in Measurement
stem: Each side of a cube is measured to be \(7.203\,\text{m}\). What are the total surface area and the volume of the cube to appropriate significant figures?
solution:
The number of significant figures in the measured length is 4. The calculated area and the volume should therefore be rounded off to 4 significant figures.

Surface area of the cube \(= 6(7.203)^{2}\,\text{m}^{2} = 311.299254\,\text{m}^{2} = 311.3\,\text{m}^{2}\)

Volume of the cube \(= (7.203)^{3}\,\text{m}^{3} = 373.714754\,\text{m}^{3} = 373.7\,\text{m}^{3}\)

subtopic: Significant Figures and Errors in Measurement
stem: \(5.74\,\text{g}\) of a substance occupies \(1.2\,\text{cm}^{3}\). Express its density by keeping the significant figures in view.
solution:
There are 3 significant figures in the measured mass whereas there are only 2 significant figures in the measured volume. Hence the density should be expressed to only 2 significant figures.

Density \(= \dfrac{5.74}{1.2}\,\text{g cm}^{-3} = 4.8\,\text{g cm}^{-3}\)

stem: Let us consider an equation \(\dfrac{1}{2} m v^{2} = m g h\) where \(m\) is the mass of the body, \(v\) its velocity, \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity and \(h\) is the height. Check whether this equation is dimensionally correct.
solution:
The dimensions of LHS are

\([\text{M}][\text{L T}^{-1}]^{2} = [\text{M}][\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}] = [\text{M L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]\)

The dimensions of RHS are

\([\text{M}][\text{L T}^{-2}][\text{L}] = [\text{M}][\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}] = [\text{M L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]\)

The dimensions of LHS and RHS are the same and hence the equation is dimensionally correct.

stem:
The SI unit of energy is \(\text{J} = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{s}^{-2}\); that of speed \(v\) is \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) and of acceleration \(a\) is \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). Which of the formulae for kinetic energy \((K)\) given below can you rule out on the basis of dimensional arguments (\(m\) stands for the mass of the body):

(a) \(K = m^{2} v^{3}\)
(b) \(K = (1/2) m v^{2}\)
(c) \(K = ma\)
(d) \(K = (3/16) m v^{2}\)
(e) \(K = (1/2) m v^{2} + ma\)
solution:
Every correct formula or equation must have the same dimensions on both sides of the equation. Also, only quantities with the same physical dimensions can be added or subtracted.

The dimensions of the quantity on the right side are \([\text{M}^{2}\text{L}^{3}\text{T}^{-3}]\) for (a); \([\text{M L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]\) for (b) and (d); \([\text{M L T}^{-2}]\) for (c). The quantity on the right side of (e) has no proper dimensions since two quantities of different dimensions have been added.

Since the kinetic energy \(K\) has the dimensions of \([\text{M L}^{2}\text{T}^{-2}]\), formulas (a), (c) and (e) are ruled out.

Note that dimensional arguments cannot tell which of the two, (b) or (d), is the correct formula. For this, one must turn to the actual definition of kinetic energy (see Chapter 5). The correct formula for kinetic energy is given by (b).

stem: Consider a simple pendulum, having a bob attached to a string, that oscillates under the action of the force of gravity. Suppose that the period of oscillation of the simple pendulum depends on its length \((l)\), mass of the bob \((m)\) and acceleration due to gravity \((g)\). Derive the expression for its time period using method of dimensions.
solution:
The dependence of time period \(T\) on the quantities \(l\), \(g\) and \(m\) as a product may be written as:

\(T = k\, l^{x} g^{y} m^{z}\)

where \(k\) is dimensionless constant and \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are the exponents.

By considering dimensions on both sides, we have

\([\text{L}^{0}\text{M}^{0}\text{T}^{1}] = [\text{L}^{1}]^{x}\,[\text{L}^{1}\text{T}^{-2}]^{y}\,[\text{M}^{1}]^{z} = \text{L}^{x+y}\,\text{T}^{-2y}\,\text{M}^{z}\)

On equating the dimensions on both sides, we have

\(x + y = 0;\quad -2y = 1;\quad \text{and } z = 0\)

So that \(x = \dfrac{1}{2},\; y = -\dfrac{1}{2},\; z = 0\)

Then, \(T = k\, l^{1/2} g^{-1/2}\), or \(T = k\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}\)

Note that value of constant \(k\) can not be obtained by the method of dimensions. Here it does not matter if some number multiplies the right side of this formula, because that does not affect its dimensions.

Actually, \(k = 2\pi\) so that \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}\)

Which of the following is the most precise device for measuring length :

(a) a vernier callipers with 20 divisions on the sliding scale
(b) a screw gauge of pitch \(1\,\text{mm}\) and 100 divisions on the circular scale
(c) an optical instrument that can measure length to within a wavelength of light ?
_note: The book prints only THREE alternatives (a), (b), (c) for this choose-one question, not four. Transcribed as a free-response row with the three printed choices inside the stem rather than as an MCQ: the bank's MCQ format requires exactly A-D, and inventing a fourth option would fabricate content. The printed key answers '(c)'.

A famous relation in physics relates 'moving mass' \(m\) to the 'rest mass' \(m_{0}\) of a particle in terms of its speed \(v\) and the speed of light, \(c\). (This relation first arose as a consequence of special relativity due to Albert Einstein). A boy recalls the relation almost correctly but forgets where to put the constant \(c\). He writes :

\(m = \dfrac{m_{0}}{\left(1 - v^{2}\right)^{1/2}}\)

Guess where to put the missing \(c\).
_note: The relation is printed WITHOUT the \(c\) deliberately — the missing constant is the whole point of the question. Transcribed exactly as printed; do not 'correct' it to \(1 - v^{2}/c^{2}\).
